newsitem.title: UK: French short dated bonds at risk, longs safe.
newsitem.headline: French short dated bonds at risk, longs safe.

text.p: It would take a bulldozer to move the 10-year spread between French and German yields, but the short end in France could be harmed by rumblings of discontent over policy on monetary union, analysts said on Thursday.

Bank of France council member Jean-Pierre Gerard was quoted on Thursday saying that while the franc-mark rate posed no problems, German lack of understanding on monetary and exchange rate policy could make a change in the parity necessary.
"The cracks are starting to emerge in France," said Tokyo Mitsubishi International bond strategist David Hewitt in London.

"But it's not like three or four years ago where you had massive international holdings of French bonds that had to come out," Hewitt said. French government securities (OATs) are largely held by loyal domestic investors now rather than the more fickle foreign buyers.

Economists said that Gerard's comments, which came in a newspaper interview and follow similar noises of discontent about currency policy from fellow council member Paul Marchelli earlier in the week, did not herald a franc devaluation.

Marchelli and Gerard said the dollar should be stronger against European currencies and Marchelli said it would be a mistake to launch EMU with too strong a euro. Meanwhile German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said devaluation talk was harmful to EMU.
Those sort of mixed signals could see shorter-dated French debt come under pressure.
"The bond market remains safe," said Nathalie Fillet, analyst at Paribas in Paris. "The risk is more on the short part of the curve, on the PIBOR contract and on the currency."
The OAT/Bund spread remained rock-solid at zero at 1220 GMT.

But French three-month futures reflect interest rates some 30 basis points above German rates, and the December and March PIBOR contracts were both lagging Euromark futures by one to two basis points on Thursday.
"It will take a great deal more of a shock on the fundamentals to change the status quo for the bonds," said Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.

Islam and others said domestic investors were unlikely to bail out of French long-term debt in the current environment, but he argued against complacency. "It would be over-optimistic to expect no economic shock would affect the French market."

Hewitt said with supply coming in the French long end in the months ahead, OATs could underperform and build up a yield premium of 10 to 20 basis points over Bunds. But he too argued against the long end as a vehicle for any French asset bears.
"If people are going to go short, they're going to go short the currency rather than the bonds."
One side-effect from the French policy comments on Wednesday may be a new note of unease about high-yielders, particularly Italy, analysts said.

Gerard said it would be a mistake to launch the euro under European monetary union, due in 1999, without Italy. But that may not sit well with German authorities and may open divisions in a previously united Franco-German political front.
Islam said Kohl is completely committed to EMU.

"But even he would have a difficult sell to the German public to allow Italy in at the start," he said. "There is a consensus that Italy should be allowed in, but perhaps with a few years more of convergence."
Hewitt too said the high-yield angle from the Gerard comments was potentially more important than the French one. "We've already seen quite a big widening already in Spain and Italy," he said.
The 10-year BTP/Bund gap was at 188 basis points, up from as low as 167 on Monday after the lira rejoined the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
